messages.subject: [statnet_help] MPLE and large networks/models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin.  Just wanted to give you an update.  I hope you don't mind  
I'm forwarding this to the list; I thought others might find this  
discussion helpful.  (A bit of background for others:  Kevin is trying  
to fit an ERGM with 71 terms on a directed network with 736 nodes.   
Four of the 71 terms are "gw" terms like gwidegree etc.)

One problem that your example was causing is that it could not even  
fit an MPLE.  This is because it is a large network and you are using  
a large number of terms.  The former means means that the number of  
dyads is large; and the combination of the two means that number of  
unique rows in the matrix of change statistics (when considering a  
change in every single dyad in the network) is also very large.  We  
had written a very simplistic algorithm -- really only meant as a  
stopgap but then forgotten about, sort of like what caused the whole  
Y2K problem :) -- to check for unique rows, and it was getting  
completely bogged down by your model / network combination.  We also  
had placed a ceiling on the max number of rows, 100K, which your model/ 
network combo was exceeding and this is what I think was part of what  
led to the errors you obtained.  (Note:  Now the ceiling is a miillion  
but this can be adjusted using control.ergm(maxNumDyadTypes=xxx))

Pavel has now replaced the old row-checking algorithm, so now it works  
much faster.  However, the problem still remains that with your  
network and the model you have chosen, almost each of the 500K+  
possible dyad changes gives a unique value for the 71-dimensional  
change statistic vector.  As a result, the logistic regression used to  
find the MPLE (which is then used as the starting value for the MCMC  
MLE routine) has to deal with an enormous covariate matrix.

Actually, it turns out that there are "only" 458362 unique rows (out  
of 736*735 = 540960 possible), which means that the covariate  
(predictor) matrix for the logistic regression is 458362 x 71.  To  
find the MPLE, we use the "glm" function of R.  It turns out that this  
function is not very good with very large covariate matrices, so just  
trying to find the MPLE made my machine choke.  This is not a problem  
with ergm, which found the 458362 x 71 matrix very quickly with the  
new code; it is (I think) the fact that glm can't seem to handle a  
matrix this large.  So I guess this is sort of bad news -- we don't  
plan to rewrite "glm", which would be a lot of work, so we have to  
live with its limitations in the absence of something better.

Note, however, that simplifying the model makes a big difference in  
the number of unique rows.  For instance, can you do without some of  
the four GW terms?  These really increase the number of rows  
dramatically, since their change statistics are real-valued variables  
(as opposed to integers, which allow for lots of duplication).

Alternatively, you could try avoiding the MPLE altogether by giving an  
explicit starting value for the parameters via the "theta0" argument  
to ergm, but this is pretty hard to do without any guidance.  One  
thing that might work, though:  Fit an MPLE using all but the four gw  
terms.  Then take those parameter estimates, tack on four zeros for  
the gw terms, and use the resulting vector as the starting value for  
the MCMC MLE routine.  This should avoid the big problems with glm.  I  
tried this, and in fact it seemed to work, or at least it ran (I  
didn't check the results too thoroughly).  I'll send you the code I  
used in a separate email.

Dave

PS.  Of course, this code assumes ergm 2.0-7, a beta version of which  
(source code only) is at http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/code/

> hi again dave,
>
> so, it was with much excitement that i finally got version 2.0-6 up  
> and running the other day, and gave my analyses another shot. alas,  
> i was still unsuccessful. here are the things i tried:
>
> "test 1"- i began with a purely "structural" model, with terms for  
> edges, mutual, gwidegree, gwodegree, gwesp, and gwdsp only. very  
> large sample size, interval, etc. statnet came back with a long  
> error message that is beyond my comprehension!
>
> next, i did some fiddling around with various terms on my own  
> computer, using the default settings except maxit=1 just to see if i  
> could get anything to go through. i came across some bizarre  
> results. all of the higher-order terms seemed to work by themselves  
> (i.e. a model was successfully estimated), but when i combined the  
> terms together R shut down on me (perhaps the same thing that was  
> happening to that other woman, and what would have happened if i ran  
> "test 1" on my own machine instead of remotely). i seemed to be  
> having particular trouble with the "gwdsp" term- the "test 1" model  
> without gwdsp didn't cause R to quit.
>
> "test 2"- brought the big guns back out, and tried my comprehensive  
> model, but without gwdsp. different error message this time, "memory  
> not mapped"?
>
> "test 3"- same thing, except i think i also dropped the gwidegree  
> term, and this time went with the default settings, plus maxit=5. i  
> thought perhaps the large sample size and interval were messing  
> things up. this time the chain seemed to start, but still cut off  
> after the first iteration- another new error message.
>

<snipped>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question on interpreting goodness-of-fit diagnostics
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have some question on interpreting the goodness-of-fit diagnostics output
figures in Statnet. For example, in the plot for (edge-wise shared
partners)X(log-odds for an edge), if in the observed data (solid line),
there is a data point at the position of 8 edge-wise shared partners and
log-odds for an edge of -3.5. So, p = e^(-3.5)/ (1+ e^(-3.5)) = 0.03 Then
can I interpret it as the probability of an edge in the observed network
having 8 edge-wise shared partners is 0.03, and given the total number of
edges in the network as 483, the total number of edges that have 8 edge-wise
shared partners is about 14?


Thanks,

Mengxiao

-- 
Zhu, Mengxiao

Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Science, McCormick
School of Engineering;
Science of Networks in Communities(SONIC) Group
Northwestern University

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question on interpreting goodness-of-fit diagnostics
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mengxiao.  Yes, this is exactly right, though I would replace  
"probability of an edge in the observed network" by "proportion of  
edges in the observed network" (the former makes an implicit  
assumption about what you mean by "probability", whereas the latter is  
technically correct as is).

By the way, you can find out exactly how many edges have 8 edge-wise  
shared partners by using
summary (yournetwork ~ esp(8))

--Dave


David Hunter
Associate professor
Department of Statistics
Penn State University

messages.subject: [statnet_help] QAP double semi-partialing
messages.body_plain:
jack.iwashyna@comcast.net wrote:
> Has anyone in statnet implemented the QAP ?double semi-partialing?
> method of Dekker, Krackhardt and Snijders 2008 Pscyhometrica paper?
> If so, is there a specific routine to call it?  It wasn't obvious to
> me from the documentation.
> 

The default method in netlm is equivalent to this procedure (it just 
goes by a name they were using for it earlier).  However, the statistic 
used is still the regression coefficient, which is not pivotal.  The 
next release will use the t-statistics instead; this should give more 
robust performance under certain scenarios.

You might also try the netperm package, which provides an alternative 
approach to this kind of question.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Kevin Lewis wrote:
> FYI, i am not sure about statnet, but i know this method has been 
> available through UCINET for some time now, very easy to use. (a 30-day 
> trial version of UCINET can be downloaded free on their website.)

Yes, Steve has always kept good support for permutation tests in UCINET, 
despite their conspicuous absence from a certain well-known text. 
(Comparison of the elaboration of the former techniques to the degree of 
support within UCINET for "p*" was, at least in the 1990s, instructive 
about certain structural matters on which I will not elaborate.)

-Carter

PS. statnet history trivia: the first routine in what would become the 
sna package was netlogit, produced as a favor for someone (not me) whose 
reviewers (also not me) demanded that the author use logistic regression 
with a QAP procedure.  This was not available elsewhere at the time.  In 
practice, it's not all that clear that QAP works well in a non-OLS GLM 
context -- see the cautionary notes in the associated man page -- but 
such is the uneven march of progress.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] nodeicov question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gail.  I'm unable to duplicate your error, though I did notice that  
both "nodeicov" and "nodeocov" improperly fit an MCMC MLE by default  
when they are in a model by themselves (such a model is one example in  
which MPLE=MLE, so ergm should recognize this automatically).  This is  
a bug, and I will fix this for the next version of ergm, but it should  
not produce the error you got.

Try running these four lines of code (after loading statnet or ergm):
  data(sampson)
  set.seed(9)
  samplike %v% "test" <- rnorm(18)
  ergm(samplike ~ nodeicov("test"))

Do you get this output?
Iteration 1 of at most 3: the log-likelihood improved by 0.0009291
Iteration 2 of at most 3: the log-likelihood improved by < 0.0001
Iteration 3 of at most 3: the log-likelihood improved by 0.001819
Newton-Raphson iterations:  7
MCMC sample of size 10000 based on:
nodeicov.test
        0.2998

Monte Carlo MLE Coefficients:
nodeicov.test
        0.3070


Dave

Hi Kevin.  The fact that you're seeing a symmetric matrix when you  
type 'net3' is no cause for alarm; this is merely how undirected  
networks are represented:  Even though you see twelve ones in the  
matrix, each pair represents only a single edge in the matrix.  Of  
course, only the lower triangle is relevant, so one might well ask  
what is the point of seeing a symmetric matrix other than simple  
aesthetics.  One answer to this is that it's sometimes of interest to  
study the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix, which are guaranteed to  
be real because it's a real symmetric matrix.

As for the plot, you may have found a bug here -- I've never used  
edge.curve before (cool!), but it does appear that something fishy is  
going on here.  I'll leave this one for Carter...

Dave

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Newbie: doubled edges in undirected network?
messages.body_plain:
Zembower, Kevin wrote:
> Is my confusion just due to my inexperience with SNA and modern
> definitions of terms like 'degree' and the way the sna package is
> deliberately designed, or should the output above for Medici be 6?

Per the man page, the degree() command returns the total (aka "Freeman") 
degree by default; as also noted on the man page, 
indegree=outdegree=total degree/2 for simple graphs.  Thus, the output 
for Medici is correct.  If you want to get the graph theoretic degree, 
you can either choose "indegree" or "outdegree," or else divide the 
return value by 2.

With respect to "doubled edges" with usecurv=T, this is just the way 
that the curved edge option handles mutual dyads: they are always 
displayed with an arc going in each direction, to emphasize the fact 
that the dyad is mutual.  In an undirected graph, of course, all dyads 
are either mutual (arc in each direction) or null (no arcs) -- the way 
this is drawn is a display convention, and doesn't suggest anything deep 
or mysterious about your structure.  Generally, there's no reason to use 
usecurv with undirected graphs, but the option is left available for 
those who prefer to display their structure in this manner.

Hope that clarifies things,

-Carter

The 'graph' package has a set nice vignettes that explain hot to use it, di you try them? These are

GraphClass: Graph Design (source, pdf)
clusterGraph: clusterGraph and distGraph (source, pdf)
graph: Graph (source, pdf)
graphAttributes: Attributes for Graph Objects (source, pdf)

You should be able to convert the objects to 'network' class, or any other, by first using 'edgeMatrix' on 'graph' object which essentially returns an edge list. Then you can supply it to network(), or as.network() to create the network object.

messages.body_plain:
Hello, Micha?, thanks for responding.

I did read the vignettes, but they didn't help. So, I wrote to the R-users list, and the maintainer of the 'graph' package, Robert Gentleman, wrote back with a solution that worked perfectly:

# Assumes working installation of Bioconductor, 'graph' and 'SNAData'.
library("SNAData")        # from Bioconductor, installs 'graph' too.
data(friendship)          # Krackhardt's high-tech manager's friendships
as(friendship, "matrix")  # view the adjacency matrix
library("network")
fnet <- network(as(friendship, "matrix"))
fnet

On a tangential note, Mr. Gentleman recommended that I read and use the RBGL Bioconductor package that he maintains, to replicate the examples in Wasserman. Just briefly reading the documentation (at http://bioconductor.org/packages/2.1/bioc/vignettes/RBGL/inst/doc/RBGL.pdf) seems to indicate that this may work, in addition to sna. I'm going to try a couple of examples and see if both sna and RBGL give the same answers. I would have never thought that Bioconductor would be the proper location for SNA or graph analysis. I only learned of this by Mr. Gentleman's note.

Any thoughts from this group regarding use of RBGL to analyze social networks?

Thanks, again, for all your advice and suggestions.

-Kevin

Hi Kevin,

The 'graph' package has a set nice vignettes that explain hot to use it, di you try them? These are

GraphClass: Graph Design (source, pdf)
clusterGraph: clusterGraph and distGraph (source, pdf)
graph: Graph (source, pdf)
graphAttributes: Attributes for Graph Objects (source, pdf)

You can open them with vignette() function from R, for example vignette(graph)

You should be able to convert the objects to 'network' class, or any other, by first using 'edgeMatrix' on 'graph' object which essentially returns an edge list. Then you can supply it to network(), or as.network() to create the network object.

HTH

Best,
